advisor.summary: Section 461(l), made permanent by OBBBA, caps the aggregate net business loss a noncorporate taxpayer may deduct against nonbusiness income in any one year — $256,000 single and $512,000 joint for 2026, after OBBBA reset the inflation indexing toward the original TCJA base. The disallowed excess converts to a net operating loss carried to the following year, so the limitation is a one-year timing toll rather than a permanent disallowance — but the carryover inherits the §172 80% cap and can never shelter the loss year's own wages or portfolio income. W-2 wages are not business income for this computation, which makes the high-salary spouse paired with a big-loss business the classic trapped-loss fact pattern. The planning levers are elective: size first-year depreciation elections so the loss lands at, not over, the cap, or accelerate business income into the loss year to absorb it currently. The engine does not enforce §461(l) — this record exists so any modeled loss near the threshold is manually sanity-checked before a plan ships.
mechanics: The computation runs in aggregate across every trade or business: total business deductions minus total business income and gains, with the excess over the §461(l)(3) threshold disallowed for the year and reported on Form 461. For 2026 the thresholds are $256,000 single / $512,000 MFJ — lower than 2025, because OBBBA reset the indexing base.

Wages from employment are not attributable to a trade or business for this purpose (§461(l)(3), as clarified by the CARES Act, P.L. 116-136) — a household with $700,000 of W-2 wages cannot use them to absorb a $900,000 business loss.

Ordering matters: basis limits, the §465 at-risk rules, and the §469 passive-activity rules apply first. A loss must clear all three gates before the excess-business-loss cap even comes into play, and the binding constraint is often one of those earlier gates.

Under §461(l)(2) the disallowed amount converts to an NOL carryover the following year, where the §172 80%-of-taxable-income limitation takes over — a trapped loss recovers, but slowly, and never against the loss year's own wages or portfolio income.
Capital gains count as business income only when they arise from the trade itself; portfolio gains do nothing to absorb the loss.

The practical levers are elective-deduction sizing — electing out of bonus depreciation by class, or moderating first-year expensing, so the usable loss lands at the cap — and, where legitimate, accelerating business income into the loss year so the loss works currently instead of carrying.

authority.note: The excess business loss limitation for noncorporate taxpayers — OBBBA removed the sunset and reset the threshold indexing; the statute this record plans around.
Treats the disallowed excess as an NOL carryover to the following year — the conversion that makes this a timing cost rather than a permanent one.
At-risk and passive-activity limits run before §461(l); the review must pin down which gate actually binds.
The converted carryover lands in the NOL regime — 80% limitation, no carryback, indefinite carryforward.

The vehicle for computing and reporting the disallowed amount.

authority.cite: David E. Watson, P.C. v. United States, 668 F.3d 1008 (8th Cir. 2012)
authority.note: The reasonable-compensation boundary: any recharacterization of S corporation owner wages to manage the wage/business-income mix must survive the compensation standards this case enforces.

requirements: A projected aggregate business loss at or near the current-year threshold that has already cleared the basis, at-risk, and passive-activity gates — otherwise those limits control, not §461(l).
Accurate classification of every income item as business or nonbusiness: wages are nonbusiness, and only gains from the trade itself count as business income.
A multi-year projection — the planning question is where the loss lands, not whether it exists.
Elective deductions (bonus, first-year expensing) still open to sizing when the plan is built; the levers close once elections are filed.
risks: The engine does not enforce the §461(l) cap, so a modeled loss above the threshold overstates the current-year benefit — the reviewing advisor must cap the number manually before it reaches a client deliverable.

Misclassifying wages or portfolio gains as business income to absorb a loss is a computational position the IRS tests directly on Form 461, and the statute is young enough that no taxpayer-favorable case law softens it.

Shifting owner compensation toward K-1 income to improve the mix runs straight into S corporation reasonable-compensation enforcement — David E. Watson, P.C. v. United States, 668 F.3d 1008 (8th Cir. 2012) is the standard any recharacterization must survive.

Stacked limitations stretch recovery: the trapped loss becomes an NOL that is itself capped at 80% of taxable income, so full absorption can take several years — set the client's cash-flow expectations accordingly.
The thresholds move every year, so a plan sized to last year's figure can strand loss above this year's lower cap.
stateNotes: States that conform to federal AGI generally inherit the §461(l) limitation automatically, but several decouple from it or impose their own loss caps — confirm each state in the client's footprint before projecting any state-side benefit.

PTET interaction: a loss year offers no pass-through income to elect an entity-level tax on, so time PTET elections to the income years; trapped federal losses do not change the state PTET computation.

Missouri conforms through its federal-AGI starting point (RSMo §143.121) and imposes no separate Missouri excess-business-loss addback, so the federal disallowance and carryover flow straight into the Missouri return.
reviewChecklist: The aggregate loss is projected against the current-year threshold before any elective depreciation choice is locked in.
Basis, at-risk, and passive gates are confirmed cleared, establishing §461(l) as the genuinely binding limit.
Every modeled plan output containing a large business loss has been manually capped at the threshold before client presentation.
Form 461 is prepared and the disallowed amount reconciles into the following year's NOL schedule.
Elective deductions are sized so that no loss is stranded above the cap without a documented reason.

client.teaser: Big write-off years run into a legal ceiling — we size the loss so none of it gets stuck.
client.headline: Put a big loss year to work right away
plainEnglish: Some years a business shows a large paper loss. Often that is the plan — big equipment or property write-offs. But tax law caps how much business loss can offset your other income, like wages, in a single year. For 2026 the cap is $256,000 for singles and $512,000 for joint filers.
The cap is lower than it was in 2025. The 2025 tax law reset the numbers. And a salary does not count as business income here. So high-salary households hit the cap sooner than they expect.
Losses over the cap are not gone. They roll into future years. But waiting is slower, and usually worth less than using them now. We size and time the write-offs so the loss does its work this year.
client.analogy: Picture a drain that takes only so much water per hour. Pour faster and the extra pools up and waits. We pour at the pace the drain can handle, so nothing sits around losing value.
benefits: Big write-off years planned so the deductions land now

Any amount that carries forward is tracked and aimed at your best future years
steps: WE project the year's total loss against the cap before you commit to big purchases.
